study_identification.author_journal_year: Sun et al., Journal of Affective Disorders, 2025
study_identification.title: Dissecting heterogeneity in major depressive disorder via normative model-driven subtyping of functional brain networks

study_characteristics.study_objective: To dissect the heterogeneity in major depressive disorder (MDD) through normative model-driven subtyping of functional brain networks by quantifying individual deviations in brain network degree centrality and identifying distinct MDD subtypes characterized by unique functional brain network patterns and cognitive correlates.

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: DPARSF (Data Processing Assistant for Resting-State fMRI); GRETNA (Graph Theoretical Network Analysis Toolbox)

quality_checking_detail.answer: Exclusion criteria included: 1) excessive head motion (mean framewise displacement > 0.2 mm); 2) imaging distortions identified by visual inspection; 3) imaging signal lost in any region of interest from the Harvard-Oxford atlas cortical areas; 4) sites with fewer than 10 MDD patients or 10 HC subjects were excluded to ensure adequate sample size and minimize extreme biases

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: Hierarchical Bayesian regression (HBR) was employed to develop normative models that accommodate site-related variability. HBR allows for the imposition of a common prior distribution across multiple sites to estimate site-specific yet interrelated means and variances, thus accommodating signal and noise variability in multisite data while preserving meaningful site-related variations. Site 4 and Site 25 were excluded (Site 4 had duplicated participants with Site 14, and Site 25 contained excessive late-onset depression cases and remitted patients).

response_variable.answer: Degree centrality (area under the curve, AUC) of brain functional networks across 96 brain regions defined by the Harvard-Oxford atlas

predictor_effects.answer: HBR allows for modeling site-specific yet interrelated means and variances with a common prior distribution across multiple sites (fixed effects: age and sex; random effects: site)

HBR is specifically described as accommodating signal and noise variability in multisite data while preserving meaningful site-related variations. Preprocessing includes nuisance regression to remove motion parameters, white matter signals, and CSF signals. The validation demonstrates that site variability is handled through 10-fold cross-validation stratified by site. Model fit metrics (SMSE and MSLL) show appropriate handling of variance structure.

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: To minimize the impact of site-related variability on subsequent results, hierarchical Bayesian regression (HBR) was employed in the HC cohort to develop a normative model of network degree centrality as a function of age and sex for each brain region. HBR allows for the imposition of a common prior distribution across multiple sites to estimate site-specific yet interrelated means and variances, thus accommodating signal and noise variability in multisite data while preserving meaningful site-related variations. The nuisance regression was conducted to remove Friston-24 motion parameters, white matter signals, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) signals. Specifically, we stratified the entire HC dataset by site and randomly divided it into 10 folds. The overall standardized mean squared error was close to 1 (1.014 ± 0.005), and the mean squared log-loss was close to 0 (0.001 ± 0.004).

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason:
The paper performs 10-fold cross-validation on the healthy control (HC) dataset, which represents validation using the same domain (healthy controls) with non-independent data. Each fold is used for training (9 folds) and testing (1 fold) iteratively. This validation strategy uses overlapping data from the same HC cohort across folds. The cross-validation is stratified by site to maintain the site distribution. Model performance metrics (SMSE and MSLL) are computed from this validation.
EXTRAS: {"summary": "10-fold cross-validation performed on the healthy control dataset with stratification by site. Each fold used for training (9 folds) and testing (1 fold) iteratively. Overall SMSE close to 1 (1.014 ± 0.005) and MSLL close to 0 (0.001 ± 0.004)."}
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: To evaluate the generalizability of the normative models, we first performed normative modeling on the HC using 10-fold cross-validation, and assessed the models using overall normalized mean squared error and mean squared log-loss. Specifically, we stratified the entire HC dataset by site and randomly divided it into 10 folds. In each modeling iteration, we used 9 folds to train the models, with the remaining 1 fold serving as the test set to evaluate the models' generalizability. This process was repeated 10 times to ensure that each fold was excluded once. The 10-fold cross-validation performed on the HC revealed the high generalizability of the normative models' fitting performance. The overall standardized mean squared error was close to 1 (1.014 ± 0.005), and the mean squared log-loss was close to 0 (0.001 ± 0.004), see Fig. S2.

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason:
The paper does not describe validation using an independent healthy control dataset separate from the training data. After 10-fold cross-validation on the HC data, the normative models were trained on all HC data and later applied to MDD patients. All healthy control data is used for model training after cross-validation. There is no mention of holding out a completely independent HC test set. The limitations section acknowledges: although the sample size of this study was commendable, our findings have not yet been validated with external data from different populations.
EXTRAS: {"summary": "No validation using an independent healthy control dataset separate from the training data. All HC data used for model training after cross-validation. The limitations section acknowledges findings have not been validated with external data from different populations."}
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: Then, the normative models were trained on all HC data and later applied to MDD patients. Secondly, although the sample size of this study was commendable, our findings have not yet been validated with external data from different populations. To enhance the reliability and broaden the applicability of our subtype classification, upcoming research ought to incorporate a more diverse participant pool.

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason:
The paper applies the normative model trained on HC data to MDD patients, which represents a different clinical domain. However, this is not a traditional validation but rather the main application of the model. The paper does validate robustness using a different atlas (AAL90 vs. Harvard-Oxford), which shows consistency of findings across different measurement domains. High correlations were found between atlases (r = 0.681-0.823, all p < 0.001) and clustering overlap rate was 0.726 between atlases. However, there is no validation using a completely independent external dataset from different sites/populations. The limitations explicitly state: our findings have not yet been validated with external data from different populations.

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: To assess the robustness of our findings across different brain atlases, we replicated the analysis using the AAL90 atlas (details in Supplementary Materials). To verify the robustness of our findings, we further employed the AAL90 atlas to follow the same analysis process and compared whether the patterns of degree centrality deviations and clustering results were consistent across the two atlases. The correlation analysis revealed high consistency in the deviation patterns across all seven functional brain networks between the two atlases (Table S2) with correlations ranging from 0.681 to 0.823. We found an overall overlap rate of 0.726, with an overlap rate of 0.701 for subtype 1 and 0.758 for subtype 2, suggesting that despite some anatomical parcellation differences between brain atlases, the classification of MDD subtypes showed high stability across different atlases. Secondly, although the sample size of this study was commendable, our findings have not yet been validated with external data from different populations.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.location: Section 2.2 (line 80), Supplementary Materials Validation analysis section (lines 25-31), Section 4 Discussion (line 244)

clinical_groups_age.answer: All MDD: mean 35.167 ± 11.950 (range 18-65 years); Subtype 1: mean 34.537 ± 12.229; Subtype 2: mean 35.936 ± 11.571

deviation_metric.answer: Z-score metric derived by normalizing the difference between actual and predicted degree centrality based on prediction uncertainty. Formula: z_ij calculated from predicted degree centrality, actual degree centrality, predictive uncertainty, and normative variance. Threshold of ± 2.6 (equivalent to p < 0.005) used to detect individual-level outliers.

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: One-sample t-tests on deviation values of all regions for each subtype to assess statistical significance (Bonferroni correction); Two-sample t-tests comparing brain network deviations between subtypes; Pearson correlation analyses between deviation values and HAMD scores (FDR correction); Partial least squares (PLS) regression to explore spatial correlations between cognitive functions and observed deviations; Permutation tests (10,000 permutations) with spatial-autocorrelation correction to determine significance of PLS components
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Two distinct MDD subtypes were identified with opposing patterns of network topology between unimodal and transmodal networks, each associated with distinct clinical presentations and cognitive profiles.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Subtype 1 (55% of patients) exhibited positive deviations in degree centrality in the limbic (LIM), frontoparietal (FPN), and default mode networks (DMN), but negative deviations in visual (VIS) and sensorimotor networks (SMN), with positive correlations to higher cognitive functions (memory retrieval, emotion regulation, impulsivity) and negative correlations to basic perceptual processes. Subtype 2 (45% of patients) demonstrated opposing patterns with negative deviations in LIM, FPN, and DMN, and positive deviations in VIS and SMN, along with inverse cognitive associations (positive loadings on motor functions, pain, imagery). Subtype 2 exhibited significantly higher onset age (t = 2.286, p = 0.023) and more severe general somatic symptoms (t = 2.169, p = 0.031) and hypochondriasis (t = 2.290, p = 0.023) compared to subtype 1. In subtype 2, deviation values of right posterior inferior temporal gyrus and LIM were negatively correlated with HAMD scores (ITGpost.R: r = -0.184, corrected p = 0.013; LIM: r = -0.139, corrected p = 0.025).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: 1) Cross-sectional design limits capacity to observe long-term associations and establish causal relationships; longitudinal studies needed to validate stability of subtypes. 2) Findings not yet validated with external data from different populations; more diverse participant pools needed. 3) Incomplete clinical information for certain MDD patients (first-episode status, medication usage) constrained thorough assessment of these factors. 4) Cognitive functions analyzed at group level; future research should examine individual-level relationships between brain function abnormalities and cognitive functions.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: K-means clustering algorithm used with Silhouette Index and Calinski-Harabasz Index to determine optimal cluster number (k = 2); Neurosynth meta-analytic platform used to analyze cognitive correlates using 117 cognitive terms from Cognitive Atlas; Degree centrality calculated at network sparsity threshold ranging from 0.05 to 0.50 at 0.01 intervals; area under curve (AUC) used as summarized scalar; Subgroup analyses confirmed medication use and episode status (first vs. recurrent) did not significantly affect subtype deviation patterns; Fisher's z-transformation applied to Pearson correlation coefficients for functional connectivity matrices; Harvard-Oxford atlas (96 regions) used for primary analysis; AAL90 atlas used for validation; Brain regions assigned to seven Yeo networks: VIS, SMN, DAN, VAN, LIM, FPN, DMN; Positive outliers ranged from 0.1255% to 1.6311%; negative outliers ranged from 0.1255% to 1.2547% across all MDD patients; Spatial overlap rate for outliers was more consistent within subtypes than across entire MDD cohort
